video.title: Samples and uncertainty: Every sample wobbles
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Charts draw themselves; code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Amina Bello - primary teacher, Nigeria (main character)
Narrator - the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.narration: Two teachers asked forty pupils each how long they spend on homework. One found fifty minutes and the other found sixty. Was one of them wrong?
Today: why a sample never gives exactly the right answer, and how wrong it might be.
The population is everyone we care about, say all eight hundred pupils. A sample is the group we actually ask. We use the sample to estimate something about the whole population.
Pick forty pupils at random and you get one average. Pick another forty and you get a slightly different one. Neither teacher was wrong, because every random sample wobbles around the true value.
We took twenty random samples from the school records and plotted their averages. Most land between fifty and sixty minutes, around the true value of fifty five.
So we report a range, not one number. We say fifty five minutes, plus or minus five. A bigger sample shrinks the margin, but four times as many pupils only halves it.
A big sample can still be wrong if it is not random. If we only ask pupils who stay after school, we miss those who leave early to work. Always ask who was left out.
Quick check! Two random samples of forty pupils give fifty and sixty minutes. What is the best explanation?
Random samples vary, so both answers are reasonable. Together they suggest the true value is somewhere near fifty five. A range tells that story honestly.
In the app, open the sampling lab. Draw many samples, then make each sample bigger, and watch the averages crowd closer together.
Your turn. We want a smaller margin of error. What should we do?
Ask more pupils, chosen at random. Remember: samples wobble, so report a range, and check who your sample left out.
Try it in class tomorrow: put sixty numbered cards in a bag, and let each group draw ten and find the average. Write every group's average on the board and ask: why are they all different?

checkpoints.prompt: Two random samples of 40 pupils give 50 and 60 minutes. What is the best explanation?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: every random sample wobbles around the true value.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: two fair samples can easily differ by chance.

checkpoints.prompt: We want a smaller margin of error. What should we do?

options.text: Ask more pupils, chosen at random

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: a bigger random sample wobbles less.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: only more randomly chosen pupils shrink the margin.
